automation_evidence.finding: Controlled experiment: developers given an AI pair programmer finished a standardized coding task 55.8% faster than the control group, with larger relative gains for less-experienced participants. Small sample of recruited developers doing one HTTP-server task, so external validity to messy client work is limited.
automation_evidence.study_type: peer-review-track preprint (arXiv 2302.06590, Microsoft/GitHub/MIT-affiliated authors) - randomized controlled experiment

automation_evidence.finding: RCT with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 real tasks in mature repos: allowing early-2025 AI tools increased task completion time by 19%, even though developers predicted a 20% speedup. Evidence that gains do not automatically transfer to complex, high-standard, existing codebases.
automation_evidence.study_type: peer-review-track preprint (arXiv 2507.09089, METR) - randomized controlled trial

automation_evidence.finding: LLM-generated unit tests (TestPilot, 25 npm packages, 1,684 API functions) reached 70.2% median statement coverage and 52.8% branch coverage, versus 51.3% / 25.6% for a prior feedback-directed tool - i.e., test authoring, a core QA hotspot, is partly automatable today.

Staggered rollout of a generative-AI assistant to 5,179 customer-support agents raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average (34% for novice/low-skilled agents, minimal for experts) and improved customer sentiment and retention. Closest large-scale analogue to help-desk/ticket work rather than an IT-specific study.
automation_evidence.study_type: peer-reviewed (NBER Working Paper 31161; published in Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025)

automation_evidence.finding: Task-level exposure: ~80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected by LLMs and ~19% at least 50%; with LLM-powered software, 47-56% of all tasks could be done significantly faster at the same quality. Exposure estimate, not a measured productivity outcome.
automation_evidence.study_type: academic working paper (arXiv 2303.10130, Eloundou et al.)

automation_evidence.finding: Prototype using real technical-incident data from a Swiss telecoms operator: GPT-4 could automate lower-level cognitive tasks in technical customer service (translation, summarization, content generation), while higher-level reasoning needed retrieval-augmentation or fine-tuning. Qualitative feasibility, no time-saved measurement.
automation_evidence.study_type: peer-reviewed conference paper (Spring Servitization Conference 2024; arXiv 2405.09161)

automation_evidence.finding: Vendor evaluation of 100+ LLMs across Java, Python, C#, JavaScript: 45% of generated code samples failed security tests and introduced OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities (Java 72%); security performance stayed flat as models improved on functional correctness. Supports a mandatory human-review/verification gate on generated code.
automation_evidence.study_type: vendor research (Veracode 2025 GenAI Code Security Report)

automation_evidence.finding: DORA's 2025 industry study frames AI chiefly as an amplifier of an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, with returns depending more on the surrounding delivery system than on tool choice. Directional, no effect size taken from the page opened.

common_tools: Remote monitoring and management (RMM) agents/consoles: ConnectWise Automate, Kaseya VSA (incl. Datto RMM), N-able, NinjaOne, Atera, ScreenConnect, ManageEngine RMM Central
Professional services automation (PSA) / ticketing and billing: ConnectWise Manage, Datto Autotask, HaloPSA, plus ITSM suites such as ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Freshservice, Zendesk
Documentation/knowledge bases and credential vaults used to ground support answers and runbooks
Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, Intune, Defender; Azure, AWS, Google Workspace admin consoles
Endpoint security and backup consoles (EDR such as SentinelOne / CrowdStrike / Microsoft Defender; backup such as Veeam / Datto)
Source control and CI: GitHub / GitLab, Jira / Azure DevOps, VS Code with Copilot / Cursor / Claude Code-style assistants
Accounting/billing and time tracking (e.g., QuickBooks) that PSA billing and utilization reporting must reconcile with
constraints: Client-health-data exposure: MSPs supporting healthcare, pharma and life-sciences clients handle PHI and are typically bound by HIPAA Security Rule obligations through business associate agreements; prompts, logs and model endpoints must stay inside the covered boundary (business-associate framing is general regulatory knowledge; the primary HHS/eCFR pages returned 403 during this research - see data_gaps).
Payment-card data: PCI DSS scoping for retail/hospitality SMB clients limits where cardholder data can be sent, which usually rules out public LLM endpoints for ticket text containing card data.

Regulated-vertical contracts: financial-services clients (GLBA safeguards, SEC/FINRA-style recordkeeping and supervision) and legal clients (attorney-client confidentiality, privilege, litigation hold) frequently contractually forbid sending matter data to third-party model providers.

Defense-industrial-base clients: NJ has a significant defense/aerospace supplier base, bringing CMMC/DFARS-style controls on controlled unclassified information - inference from the client mix, not measured here.

Privileged tooling: RMM agents run with high-level access to client networks and endpoints and are themselves a known attack surface, so agentic automation acting through RMM must be scoped, logged and human-approved for write actions.
Multi-tenant data segregation: an MSP stores many clients' data in one PSA/RMM/documentation stack, so retrieval and fine-tuning must enforce per-client isolation to avoid cross-client leakage.

IP, licensing and code provenance: AI-generated code raises open-source license contamination, warranty/indemnity and deliverable-ownership questions in fixed-fee custom-development contracts - inference from standard contract practice.
Insurance/cyber-underwriting and client security questionnaires increasingly require disclosure of AI subprocessors and data flows.
Accessibility and sector rules (e.g., WCAG expectations in government/education custom software) still require human sign-off on AI-drafted UI and content.
trends: Help desk/service desk is the core MSP service line, not an add-on: a 2024 Channel Futures MSP 501 survey cited on Wikipedia found 93% of respondents offered help desk/service desk support versus 88% offering RMM - the largest addressable automation surface is ticket work (secondary source, treat as indicative).

Entry-level squeeze: using ADP payroll microdata through June 2026, employment of 22-25 year-olds in AI-exposed occupations sits ~19% below its counterfactual, driven by reduced hiring rather than separations, with no comparable gap for experienced workers (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, revised August 2026; descriptive, not causal).

NJ pay is discounted versus the New York side of the metro: 2025 OEWS medians for software developers are $135,940 statewide versus $166,830 in the NY-Newark-Jersey City metro, which contains Middlesex County - local firms compete for the same talent pool at a discount, pressuring utilization and margin (inference from wage differential).

Tool consolidation toward AI-native PSA/RMM: RMM is now predominantly SaaS and vendors have been adding AI/ML for anomaly detection and automation since the 2020s, so new agents must integrate with incumbent PSA/RMM consoles rather than replace them (Wikipedia RMM overview citing vendor and market sources).

Tooling market growth: RMM SaaS estimated at ~$5.4B globally in 2024 with forecasts above $12B by 2033, and PSA software ~$12.4B in 2024 forecast to $40.3B by 2033 - third-party market-research figures, low reliability, useful only for direction.

Task-level exposure is broad rather than confined to coding: ~80% of US workers could see at least 10% of tasks affected by LLMs, with higher-wage occupations more exposed (Eloundou et al.), which is why documentation, status reporting and triage matter as much as code generation.
caveats: Wage figures are May 2025 OEWS estimates as republished by O*NET because bls.gov OEWS HTML tables redirected and the BLS Public Data API was rate-limited during this research; O*NET states the source as BLS 2025 wage data, but the figures were not read off a BLS table directly. OEWS data are occupation-based, not industry-based: no NAICS 5415 (computer systems design and related services) wage or employment series was obtained, so these are wages for the occupations these firms employ, not for the firms themselves. Middlesex County sits inside the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area used here; O*NET/OEWS did not publish a separate Edison-New Brunswick figure in the tables opened (inference on county-to-metro mapping). Manual task hotspots are occupation-level O*NET task statements, which describe what workers do in general, not what a particular MSP's ticket queue looks like, and no time-share or volume weighting is attached. The automation evidence is skewed toward code writing and general customer support: the large-sample studies (Brynjolfsson et al.) are about contact-center agents, not IT help desks, and the IT/ITSM-specific literature found was prototype-scale and reported feasibility rather than measured hours saved. The two strongest code-productivity results point in opposite directions (55.8% faster in a greenfield single-task experiment; 19% slower for experienced developers on mature repos), so any ROI claim should be scoped to task type and codebase maturity. Veracode and DORA are vendor/industry sources and rated Low. The common_tools list combines vendor categories named on the RMM and PSA reference pages with general industry knowledge; no single authoritative product census was opened. The constraints list reflects standard regulatory and contracting practice for regulated verticals; primary regulatory text could not be retrieved (HHS/eCFR returned 403), so treat constraint wording as design guidance rather than legal citation. No NJ- or Middlesex-specific automation study, MSP margin survey or seasonality data was found.
data_gaps: No NAICS 5415 wage, employment or establishment counts for New Jersey or Middlesex County: bls.gov QCEW/OEWS pages redirected and the BLS API was rate-limited; NJ LWD dashboards are Power BI/Power BI Gov apps that could not be extracted.
No County- or metro-division-level wage data for Edison-New Brunswick: used the New York-Newark-Jersey City MSA as the local proxy.

No credible, quantified study of AI time savings in MSP help-desk ticket triage was located; arXiv searches for service-desk/ITSM LLM work returned network-management papers, not measured deflection or handle-time results.

MSP industry surveys (Channel Futures MSP 501, CompTIA State of the Tech Workforce, vendor MSP surveys) were not opened directly - only secondhand through reference pages - so no primary MSP-specific labor-shortage or margin statistics are reported.
Vendor/productivity claims from GitHub, Microsoft, ServiceNow and similar (e.g., percentage of tickets resolved by AI agents) were deliberately excluded as unverifiable marketing.
Seasonality, project-spike patterns and bench/utilization swings for NJ IT services firms were not quantified from any source.
HIPAA (hhs.gov 403), eCFR (federalregister.gov request-access block) and PCI DSS primary texts were not retrievable, so regulatory constraints rest on general knowledge rather than opened sources.
No NJ-specific data on AI adoption rates among IT services firms; the national Census BTOS AI supplement was not extracted.
